currentEntries.definition: Receiving God's testimony as governing truth in a response that submits to it. Bare assent can recognize a fact — demons believe and tremble — but saving belief obeys the word believed, and persistent refusal to obey exposes unbelief.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: personal trust in Christ, not mere assent — the instrument that receives salvation.
currentEntries.citations: (Mark 1:27; John 3:36; 12:42-43; Rom 10:16; Heb 3:18-19; Jas 2:19-22) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Belief is most commonly understood not as a symbolic image but as faith: accepting the truth of God’s revelation and personally trusting, relying upon, and committing oneself to God—especially to Jesus Christ—for salvation.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'belief' or 'to believe' (Greek pisteuo, Hebrew aman) is understood not as mere intellectual acknowledgment but as saving faith: personal trust in, reliance upon, and commitment to God and specifically to Jesus Christ as Lord and Savior. It is treated as the divinely appointed means of receiving salvation, justification, and eternal life, involving assent to the truth of the gospel, trust of the heart, and entrustment of oneself to Christ. Classical Protestant theology often analyzes it into three elements: notitia (knowledge of the content), assensus (assent that it is true), and fiducia (personal trust). Belief is thus the relational counterpart of God's grace: grace offers, faith receives.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Personal trust/reliance upon God (especially Jesus Christ) for salvation, eternal life, and relationship with God, going beyond mere intellectual assent to include commitment and dependence

currentEntries.definition: To cleanse is to remove the defilement that bars proper contact, approach, or use; clean describes what is free of that defilement and fit for its permitted place. Uncleanness may be physical, ceremonial, or moral and does not always mean guilt: childbirth, marital relations, and touching the dead all make unclean without being called sin. Cleansing removes what makes a vessel unfit; sanctification places the cleansed vessel under a holy claim and appointed use.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly treated either as hygiene and obsolete ritual regulation, or as a synonym for moral purity and holiness.
currentEntries.citations: (Lev 10:10; 12:2; 15:18; Num 19:11; Ps 51:2, 10; Eph 5:26; 1 John 1:7, 9) · see Uncommon Sanctification, Justification, and Cleanliness

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual and moral purity or impurity before God: “unclean” commonly symbolizes sin, defilement, and unfitness for God’s holy presence, while cleansing symbolizes forgiveness, purification, sanctification, and restoration to fellowship with God.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'clean/unclean' is understood as ritual-purity language that symbolizes moral and spiritual condition before God: uncleanness represents sin, defilement, and unfitness to approach a holy God, while cleanness represents holiness, moral purity, and acceptable standing in God's presence. Correspondingly, 'cleanse/cleansing' symbolizes God's forgiveness of sin and the sanctification of the believer, accomplished ultimately through the atoning blood of Christ (with the Old Testament washings and purification rites read as types or foreshadowings of that spiritual cleansing). A closely joined sub-theme is Jesus' relocation of defilement from external ritual to the inner heart (Mark 7), and the New Testament's declaration that former ritual categories (foods, Gentiles) are now 'cleansed,' opening covenant access to all peoples.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual and moral purity versus defilement by sin, with 'clean' denoting holiness and fitness for God's presence, 'unclean' denoting sin-induced impurity or separation from God, and 'cleansing/cleanse' denoting divine purification and forgiveness (especially through Christ's atoning blood, the Spirit, or the word), of which OT ritual categories are types.

currentEntries.definition: One in whom the law is sealed — “seal the law among my disciples” — proven by continuing in the word, love, and fruit; three times Jesus says cannot of those who will not leave their own, bear the cross, and forsake all. Baptized into the Name, the disciple is perfected “as his master” — the One in whom the Name, the covenant, and so the law dwell.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: a learner and follower of Jesus — any believer, entered by faith and baptism, growing lifelong in Christlikeness.
currentEntries.citations: (Isa 8:16; Luke 6:40; Ex 23:21; Jer 31:33; John 8:31; Luke 14:26-33; Rev 14:1) · see The Disciple, ch. 9

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A disciple most commonly signifies a committed follower and learner of Jesus—one who receives his teaching, imitates his way of life, obeys him, and participates in his mission. In Christian application, the disciple often functions as the model or representative of Christian believers generally.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'disciple' (Greek mathētēs, 'learner' or 'pupil') primarily denotes a committed follower of Jesus Christ — one who learns from him, obeys his teaching, imitates his life, and is bound to him in personal allegiance. Symbolically, discipleship stands for the whole Christian life: self-denial, cross-bearing, obedience to Jesus' word, love for fellow believers, and fruit-bearing. In this dominant reading, 'disciple' is functionally equivalent to 'Christian' (cf. Acts 11:26), describing not merely intellectual students but apprentices whose lives are being conformed to their Master.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A committed learner and follower of Jesus Christ who adheres to His teachings, imitates His way of life, and often incurs personal cost or self-denial

currentEntries.definition: A devouring kingdom.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: Satan himself, per Revelation 12:9.
currentEntries.citations: (Pharaoh, Ezek 29:3; Babylon, Jer 51:34) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Satan—the devil as the chief personal power of evil, enemy of God, accuser and persecutor of God’s people.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching the dragon is overwhelmingly understood as a symbol of Satan (the devil), the primordial adversary of God and persecutor of God's people. The Book of Revelation makes this identification explicit, calling the great red dragon 'that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan,' thereby also linking the dragon to the serpent of Eden. By extension the dragon symbolizes cosmic evil and the chaotic, God-opposing power that stands behind hostile earthly kingdoms.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Satan (the Devil), the ancient serpent and adversary of God who opposes Christ and persecutes the people of God

currentEntries.definition: Spiritually, the whore of Babylon that rides the beast — the city that kills the prophets, “where also our Lord was crucified”: Jerusalem.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: bondage to sin, and the world-system out of which God redeems.
currentEntries.citations: (Rev 11:8; 18:24; Matt 23:37; Gal 4:25; Isa 1:10) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Bondage to sin and to an oppressive, godless world-system, from which God delivers his people in an exodus. In common Christian typology, Egypt is the realm of slavery, Pharaoh represents enslaving power, and departure from Egypt prefigures salvation and liberation.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, Egypt is primarily a symbol of bondage and slavery — specifically the world of sin and oppression from which God delivers His people. The Exodus narrative is treated as the paradigm of salvation, so 'Egypt' becomes shorthand for the old life of enslavement (to sin, to the world, to worldly powers) that believers are redeemed out of, with the Exodus itself typologically foreshadowing redemption in Christ. Leaving Egypt = conversion/deliverance; longing to return to Egypt = backsliding toward the old sinful life or worldliness.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: bondage/slavery to sin and the world system opposed to God, from which God delivers His people

currentEntries.definition: Trusting faithfulness — reliance on God's unseen promise held steady through obedience. Works do not purchase the promise; they enact and bring faith to maturity, and faith without them is dead.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: confident trust in God and His promises — the sole instrument of justification.
currentEntries.citations: (Hab 2:4; Heb 11:1, 8; Jas 2:17, 22; Rom 4:4-5; Eph 2:8-10) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Trusting reliance on God—especially confidence in Jesus Christ and his saving work—expressed through commitment, obedience, and hope rather than mere intellectual agreement.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'faith' (Greek pistis, Hebrew emunah) primarily denotes personal trust in and reliance upon God — and, in the New Testament, specifically trust in Jesus Christ and his saving work — rather than mere intellectual agreement. It is standardly defined as confident assurance in God's character and promises, the divinely enabled means by which a person receives salvation and is counted righteous ('justification by faith'), and the posture of dependence that characterizes the whole Christian life ('walking by faith, not by sight').

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Trusting reliance and confident assurance in God and His promises, centered on Jesus Christ for salvation and life (not mere intellectual assent)

currentEntries.definition: A devouring kingdom that swallows and is forced to give back.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: God's appointed rescue-instrument, a type of the three days in the tomb.
currentEntries.citations: (Jer 51:34; Ezek 32:2) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian interpretation of the “great fish” in Jonah, the most recognizable symbolic reading is the realm of death or the grave from which God delivers—typologically anticipating Christ’s burial and resurrection after three days.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching the 'great fish' is understood first as God's appointed instrument of both judgment and deliverance for Jonah, and above all as a type of Christ's burial and resurrection: Jonah's three days and nights in the fish's belly prefigure Jesus' three days in the tomb, a typology Jesus himself invokes as 'the sign of Jonah.' The fish thus symbolizes divine preservation through death-like descent and the certainty of resurrection.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Typological prefiguration of Christ's death, burial for three days, and resurrection (the great fish's belly as the grave/Sheol)

currentEntries.definition: A planted stand of trees — a grouping of nations.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: paradise and fellowship with God — Eden lost and restored.
currentEntries.citations: (Ezek 31:9) · see Trees, ch. 41

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Paradise: the ordered, life-giving presence of God in which humanity enjoys communion with God, often extended to the hope of creation restored.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the garden symbolizes paradise as the place of God's presence and unbroken communion between God and humanity. Rooted in the Garden of Eden, it represents the original blessed state of creation—provision, fellowship with God, and life (the tree of life)—which is lost through sin (expulsion from Eden) and finally restored in the new creation, where Revelation deliberately returns to garden imagery (tree of life, river of life). The garden thus frames the whole canonical arc: paradise created, paradise lost, paradise regained.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The Garden of Eden as paradise: the original place of perfect creation, innocence, abundance, and unhindered communion with God, later associated with the Fall and eschatological restoration

currentEntries.definition: The rage of the wicked at the righteous — what the excluded do at the sight of the kingdom they forfeited, sorrow and hatred in one face; then they melt away. Defined on the wicked against the just, staged at Stephen's trial, templated in the psalm: he shall see, be grieved, gnash, and perish.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the anguish of the damned under conscious, everlasting torment.
currentEntries.citations: (Ps 112:10; Ps 37:12; Luke 13:28; Acts 7:54; Matt 8:12) · see The Weeping and the Gnashing | (Ps 112:10; Ps 37:12; Luke 13:28; Acts 7:54; Matt 8:12) · see The Weeping and the Gnashing, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Severe anguish, despair, and sometimes enraged regret experienced under divine judgment—especially exclusion from God’s kingdom and, in traditional Christian teaching, the punishment of hell.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'gnashing of teeth' (nearly always paired with 'weeping') symbolizes the extreme anguish, despair, and suffering of those who are excluded from God's kingdom and consigned to final judgment or hell. It functions as a stock formula in Jesus' teaching for the conscious misery and regret of the condemned — the pain of eschatological loss.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Intense anguish, sorrow, and regret experienced by those excluded from God's kingdom and consigned to eschatological punishment (outer darkness or hell)

currentEntries.definition: The gospel of the kingdom — the renewed covenant, the law going forth from Zion.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the good news that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again.
currentEntries.citations: (Isa 52:7; 2:3; Jer 31:33; Heb 4:2) · see Gospel, ch. 5

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The “Gospel” primarily means the good news that God’s saving reign has come through Jesus Christ—especially through his death and resurrection—calling people to faith, repentance, forgiveness, and new life.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'Gospel' (Greek euangelion, 'good news') primarily denotes the message of salvation accomplished by God through the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ — the announcement that God has acted in Christ to forgive sin, reconcile humanity to himself, and inaugurate his kingdom, received by faith. It is less a symbol than a technical term for the core Christian proclamation (kerygma).

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the good news of salvation through the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ

currentEntries.definition: The covenant-breaker who wears the form of covenant without its substance — “that great city,” spiritually Sodom, Egypt, Babylon: Jerusalem unfaithful.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: spiritual adultery; in Revelation, an apostate religious world-system — Rome, not Jerusalem.
currentEntries.citations: (Rev 17:18; 11:8; Ezek 23:19) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Spiritual or covenantal unfaithfulness—especially idolatry, apostasy, and reliance on corrupt political powers—is the most common symbolic meaning of “harlot.” The image portrays a people, city, or religious body abandoning loyalty to God for other gods, powers, wealth, or alliances.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the harlot is the dominant biblical symbol of spiritual unfaithfulness to God — specifically idolatry and apostasy by a people covenanted to God. Israel/Judah are repeatedly portrayed as an unfaithful wife who 'plays the harlot' by worshiping other gods and trusting foreign alliances. In the New Testament the image culminates in 'Babylon the Great, mother of harlots' (Revelation 17–18), understood as a corrupt religious, political, and economic system seducing the nations away from God. Thus 'harlot' symbolically = a covenant community or world system that abandons faithfulness to God for idolatry, worldly power, and illicit alliances.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: spiritual unfaithfulness/idolatry (covenantal adultery against God)

currentEntries.definition: Jerusalem — the navel and heart of the land.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the grave or Hades, where Christ lay three days.
currentEntries.citations: (Matt 12:40; Ezek 5:5; 38:12) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4, and The Ship

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus’ death and burial—his being in the grave or, more broadly, in the state/realm of the dead before his resurrection.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'the heart of the earth' (Matthew 12:40) is understood as a reference to Jesus' burial in the tomb/grave — and, in much traditional interpretation, his sojourn in the realm of the dead (Sheol/Hades) — during the interval between his death and resurrection. It functions as the antitype of Jonah's three days and nights in the belly of the great fish, serving as the 'sign of Jonah' that prefigures Christ's death, burial, and resurrection on the third day.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The grave, physical tomb, or the general realm of the dead (Sheol or Hades) where Jesus remained between his crucifixion and resurrection.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The grave or tomb (place of burial/death) of Jesus, paralleling Jonah's confinement in the fish as a sign of death and subsequent deliverance/resurrection

currentEntries.definition: One English word laid over two different things — Sheol/Hades, the grave that swallows righteous and wicked alike, and Gehenna, the judgment that destroys. The doctrine changes with the word beneath.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the place of eternal conscious punishment and separation from God.
currentEntries.citations: (Ps 16:10 with Matt 10:28) · see Heaven and Hell, ch. 16

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Hell most commonly signifies the final condition or realm of divine judgment: irreversible exclusion from blessed communion with God and punishment of unrepentant evil. Biblical images such as fire, outer darkness, the undying worm, and the second death express the horror and finality of that judgment, though traditions differ over how literally those images should be understood.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'Hell' primarily signifies the final state or place of divine punishment and separation from God for the unrepentant wicked after death and final judgment. It is symbolically depicted through images of unquenchable fire, darkness, weeping and gnashing of teeth, and destruction (drawing on the Greek term Gehenna, itself derived from the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a site associated with idolatrous burning and later with fiery judgment). The dominant traditional reading takes this as eternal conscious punishment and exclusion from God's presence.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The final place or state of eternal conscious punishment, torment, and separation from God for the unrighteous after judgment

currentEntries.definition: To judge, declare, or demonstrate a person, word, deed, or cause right against a question or charge; the opposite is to condemn. God answers the charge against the sinner by grace through Christ, forgiving rather than renaming ungodliness righteousness. Deeds may vindicate a claimed faith, but they cannot purchase the Judge's mercy or place God in debt.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught in Protestant theology: God's once-for-all legal declaration that a believer is righteous through Christ's imputed righteousness, received by faith apart from works.
currentEntries.citations: (Deut 25:1; Prov 17:15; Matt 11:19; Luke 7:29; Rom 3:24-26; 4:4-8; 8:33; Jas 2:21-25) · see Uncommon Sanctification, Justification, and Cleanliness, and The End of the Law for Paul's law, works, wages, and debt vocabulary

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: God’s forensic declaration that a sinner is righteous—acquitted from condemnation and placed in right standing with God—on the basis of Christ’s saving work and received through faith.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'justify/justification' is understood as a forensic (legal/courtroom) term meaning to be declared righteous before God — the act by which God acquits the sinner and counts or reckons that person righteous, on the basis of faith in Jesus Christ rather than works of the law. In classic Protestant formulation this is a declarative act in which Christ's righteousness is imputed to the believer (justification by grace alone through faith alone). It is contrasted with condemnation and treated as the reversal of the guilty verdict, grounded in Christ's atoning death and resurrection.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: God's forensic (legal) declaration that a sinner is righteous and in right standing with Him, based on faith in Christ's atoning work rather than personal merit or works of the law; often involving the imputation of Christ's righteousness

currentEntries.definition: Covenant relationship proven by obedience — the intimate “knew” of marriage; a stranger is one not known.
currentEntries.citations: (Gen 4:1; Hos 4:6; Matt 7:23; 1 John 2:3-4) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: When “know” carries theological or symbolic force, it most commonly denotes personal, experiential, and covenantal relationship—especially intimate communion with God—rather than mere possession of information. Such knowledge is often understood as involving recognition, love, trust, and obedience.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching and biblical scholarship, 'to know' (Hebrew yada'; Greek ginōskō) is overwhelmingly interpreted as denoting intimate, experiential, relational knowledge rather than mere intellectual or factual awareness. 'Knowing God' is read as personal communion and covenant relationship with Him, and being 'known' by God as His personal, saving recognition and acceptance. Eternal life itself is defined as this relational knowledge (John 17:3).

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Intimate, experiential, personal relationship or union (especially with God), as distinct from mere intellectual or propositional awareness

currentEntries.definition: Covenant existence — the life the law produces.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: Christ Himself, and the eternal life imparted to believers.
currentEntries.citations: (Deut 30:19-20; Lev 18:5; John 14:6; Matt 7:14) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine or eternal life given by God in and through Jesus Christ—salvation understood as restored communion with God, spiritually present now and fulfilled in resurrection.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'life' or 'the life' symbolically denotes eternal, divine life (Greek zoe) that comes from God and is embodied in and given through Jesus Christ — a qualitatively new spiritual existence in communion with God, as opposed to mere biological existence (bios) or spiritual death. In Johannine usage especially, Christ himself is identified as 'the life,' so the term functions both as the gift (eternal life for believers) and the giver (Christ as the source and embodiment of that life).

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ himself as the personal source, embodiment, and giver of spiritual/eternal life (zoe)

currentEntries.definition: Self-giving covenant allegiance embodied, for those under God's authority, in commandment-keeping. Obedience without love can be empty sacrifice, but claimed love that persistently refuses His commands is false — “this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments”.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: self-giving devotion or benevolence toward God and neighbor, with obedience as its necessary fruit and evidence rather than love's defining form.
currentEntries.citations: (John 14:15; 1 Cor 13:3; 1 John 4:8-10; 5:3; 2 John 4-6; Rom 13:10) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Self-giving, faithful, and sacrificial concern for the good of another, grounded supremely in God’s own character and revealed in Christ. In Christian teaching, love commonly signifies both God’s gracious action toward humanity and the central obligation to love God and one’s neighbor.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'love' (especially Greek agape) primarily signifies the essential nature and character of God Himself—self-giving, sacrificial, unconditional benevolence supremely revealed in Christ's atoning death—which believers are commanded to reflect toward God and neighbor. It is treated as the summary of the Law, the greatest of the theological virtues, and the defining mark of Christian discipleship, rather than as an emotion or mere affection.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The essence and nature of God expressed as selfless, unconditional, sacrificial love (agape) that defines Christian virtue, the greatest commandment, and the model for all human relationships

currentEntries.definition: The faithful witness — the Son, who shines with no light of His own but the Father's reflected, the light that shineth in the world's night; the lesser light that rules the night and marks the appointed times.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the church reflecting Christ's light as the moon reflects the sun.
currentEntries.citations: (Ps 89:37; Rev 1:5; John 1:5; 5:19) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: In prophetic and apocalyptic interpretation, the moon most commonly functions as part of the divinely ordered cosmos; its darkening, turning to blood, or otherwise failing symbolizes the Day of the Lord, divine judgment, and the upheaval of the present world order.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In the broadest stream of Christian teaching, the moon is most commonly interpreted as the 'lesser light' that has no light of its own but reflects the light of the sun — symbolically, the Church (or the individual believer) reflecting the light of Christ, who is figured by the sun. This reading runs from patristic writers (e.g., Augustine, Ambrose, Origen) through medieval and modern devotional teaching. Bound up with this is the moon's role as a fixed, faithful witness in the heavens, a sign of God's ordered creation and covenant faithfulness.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the Church (or people of God) as a lesser light reflecting the light of Christ/the Sun

currentEntries.definition: The covenant identity of a house, consisting of 3 things appointed and provided by its Head: the Word (the manna), the covenant law (the stone tables), and the fruitful priesthood (Aaron's budded rod). A counterfeit Name substitutes a different word, covenant, or priesthood; a Name is taken in vain when any one is rejected, replaced, or removed. A bride takes her Husband's Name by entering His house, coming under His authority, and obeying Him.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the person's character, authority, and reputation.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A “name” most commonly symbolizes the identity and revealed character of the person who bears it; in biblical usage it can therefore represent the person himself or herself, including that person’s presence, reputation, and authority. God’s name especially signifies God as revealed and made known.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching and biblical interpretation, a 'name' symbolizes the essential character, identity, and authority of the person who bears it — not merely a label. Above all, the 'name of God' (or 'the name of the LORD' / 'the name of Jesus') stands for God's revealed nature, reputation, presence, and power, so that to know, call on, trust, hallow, or act 'in' the name is to engage with the person himself. Names in Scripture are consistently treated as disclosing or determining who someone truly is, which is why God's self-revelation, divine name-changes, and prayer/salvation 'in the name' carry such theological weight.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The name of a person (especially God or Jesus) stands for their full identity, character, authority, power, and presence, so that invoking or acting 'in the name' means acting by that person's authority and under their protection.

currentEntries.definition: The renewed covenant, known — kept — only by the one who receives it.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: a new God-given identity and character bestowed on the overcomer.
currentEntries.citations: (Gen 32:28; Isa 62:2-5; 65:15; Rev 2:17) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A “new name” most commonly symbolizes a new, God-given identity and status—often associated with transformation, belonging to God, vindication, and a new vocation or destiny.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, a 'new name' symbolizes the new identity, character, and status God confers on a person He has redeemed and claimed as His own. It marks a decisive transformation of the person's nature and relationship to God — the old identity is replaced by a God-given one — and, eschatologically, it signifies the believer's full acceptance, ownership by God, and glorified identity in the age to come.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A new spiritual identity or transformed character bestowed by God on the faithful/overcomer, signifying redemption, intimate belonging, and eternal status before Him

currentEntries.definition: The commandment's truth and correction received and laid up inwardly until they govern the life — the tested, pressed fruit of the Spirit stored as proven obedience; light is that obedience made visible as an example to others.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the Holy Spirit — anointing, consecration, and empowering.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The Holy Spirit—especially the Spirit’s indwelling presence, empowering, illumination, and sustaining work—is the symbolic meaning most commonly assigned to lamp oil in Christian typological and devotional teaching.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In popular Christian teaching, lamp oil is most commonly interpreted as a symbol of the Holy Spirit (or the indwelling presence/anointing of the Spirit in the believer's life), especially in expositions of the parable of the ten virgins, where having oil represents genuine Spirit-filled spiritual life and lacking it represents empty, merely external religion.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: the Holy Spirit (as the empowering, anointing presence of God that enables spiritual light, illumination, and readiness)

currentEntries.definition: The one complete light — under the KJV's “rubies” (peninim, Strong's pearl), wisdom and the bride are priced above pearls; and the night sky's one pearl is the full moon (keseh, “fulness,” the letters under “throne” and “time appointed”), governor of the appointed times, the one-pearl gates of the city — the merchant's entry at the King's gate.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the kingdom of heaven, worth surrendering everything to gain — or the church, purchased by Christ.
currentEntries.citations: (Prov 3:15; 31:10; Ps 81:3; Prov 7:20; Job 26:9; Ps 104:19; Rev 21:21) · see The Pearls of Wisdom, ch. 31

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The pearl most commonly symbolizes the incomparable worth of the kingdom of God—and, by extension, salvation or life in Christ—worth surrendering everything else to obtain.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: The pearl primarily symbolizes the Kingdom of Heaven (or the salvation/gospel found in it) as a treasure of supreme, surpassing worth — something so valuable that a person should gladly give up everything else to obtain it. By extension it stands for sacred, precious spiritual truth.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The kingdom of heaven (or the gospel of salvation/Christ) as a treasure of supreme, inestimable worth for which everything else should be sacrificed

currentEntries.definition: Right-living. God is Right-Living by definition — His ways and works are the measure of right. For those under His authority, right-living is the doing of His commandments: the law kept, worn as the garment of righteous acts. Romans 4 excludes wage-work that would put God in debt, not obedience; even complete obedience earns no wage because the servant has only done his duty. Righteousness is given and reckoned by grace, but the gift never renames wrong-living right.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: primarily right standing before God — Christ's imputed righteousness received by faith apart from works — with right-living as its subsequent fruit and evidence.
currentEntries.citations: (Deut 32:4; 6:25; Ps 119:172; 145:17; Luke 17:7-10; Rom 4:4-8; Phil 3:9; Heb 11:8; 1 John 3:7) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6, for the dependent definitions; The End of the Law for Paul's wage, debt, law, and obedience vocabulary; and Garments & Armor, ch. 43, for righteousness given and worn

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Moral and spiritual rightness before God: conformity to God’s character and will, including just conduct and, in salvation contexts, a right standing with God granted by grace.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'righteousness' primarily signifies right standing before God — a state of being in right relationship with Him and conformed to His moral character and standard. In its most prominent (especially Protestant) doctrinal use, it refers to the righteousness of God credited or imputed to believers through faith in Christ (justification), rather than righteousness achieved by human works. Symbolically it is frequently pictured as a garment or robe (clothing the sinner), a breastplate (protection), and a crown or reward, all conveying a status conferred by God that covers, protects, and vindicates the believer.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Right standing with God (justification) and conformity to God's moral standards/will, often as a gift received by faith rather than earned by works

currentEntries.definition: To cause, appoint, or acknowledge as holy — removing someone or something from common status, placing it under an owner's claim for an appointed purpose, and treating or preparing it accordingly. God sanctifies by claiming for Himself and fitting for His use; people sanctify God and His Name by treating and displaying Him as holy. Moral cleansing and obedient living fit a person to that holy calling, but they are not the word's entire meaning.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: God's progressive work of inward renewal, by which believers die more and more to sin and live in righteousness.
currentEntries.citations: (Ex 13:2; Num 8:17; Isa 8:13; Ezek 36:23; John 10:36; 17:19; 1 Cor 7:14; 1 Thess 4:3-7; 2 Tim 2:21; Heb 10:10, 29) · see Uncommon Sanctification, Justification, and Cleanliness

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Being made holy for God: set apart as belonging to God, cleansed from sin, and transformed toward holy conduct and Christlike character. In much Christian teaching, “sanctification” especially denotes the Holy Spirit’s continuing work of moral and spiritual renewal in believers.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, to 'sanctify' means to set apart as holy for God, and 'sanctification' denotes the process (and in some texts the accomplished state) by which believers are made holy — separated from sin and common use, consecrated to God, and progressively conformed to the moral character of Christ through the work of the Holy Spirit. The dominant systematic formulation, especially in Protestant theology, treats sanctification as the ongoing transformation of the believer's life that follows and is distinct from justification, culminating in glorification.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: To set apart as holy unto God or to make holy (ceremonially, positionally, or progressively) by divine action, especially the Holy Spirit's work conforming believers to Christ

currentEntries.definition: An earthly kingdom, city, state, or governed political body riding upon the sea of peoples: its rulers guide it, its inhabitants and servants crew it, its armies defend it, and its wealth is carried as cargo. Christ needs no constructed body beneath Him: He walks upon the sea directly, and when He sails with His disciples the vessel comes under its true Head. The ship may be broken while its people survive.

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The Church—often called the ship or Barque of Peter—carrying believers through the dangers of the world toward salvation, with Christ as protector or pilot.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: The ship most commonly symbolizes the Church — the vessel of salvation that carries believers safely through the storms and dangers of the world (the 'sea') toward the safe harbor of eternal life. This reading is deeply rooted in patristic writing (e.g., Tertullian, Hippolytus, Cyprian, Augustine), in liturgical architecture (the main body of a church building is called the 'nave,' from Latin navis, ship), and in the typological link between Noah's ark and baptism/the Church.

judges.label: Gemini
judges.consensusMeaning: The Church, often traditionally conceptualized as the 'Barque of Peter' or typologically linked to Noah's Ark, which carries the faithful safely through the turbulent and dangerous waters of the world toward salvation.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: The Church as the vessel of salvation navigating the waters of the world, storms of trial, or judgment (often linked to Noah's ark as type)

currentEntries.definition: A prophecy given in advance — often a prophet's lived story — whose fulfillment testifies; not a wonder performed on demand.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: a miraculous act pointing to God's power and Christ's identity.
currentEntries.citations: (Isa 7:14; Ezek 24:24; Luke 11:30) · see Signs and Similitudes, ch. 3

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A “sign” is most commonly understood functionally as a visible event, act, object, or miracle that points beyond itself to divine activity and confirms God’s message, promise, presence, or the authority of God’s messenger. It does not have one fixed symbolic referent across Scripture.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, a 'sign' (Hebrew 'oth, Greek semeion) is understood as a visible act, event, or object that points beyond itself to God's presence, power, and purpose — most characteristically a miraculous work that authenticates God's messenger and reveals divine identity. The paradigmatic usage is in John's Gospel, where Jesus' miracles are called 'signs' precisely because their significance lies not in the wonder itself but in what they disclose about who Jesus is (his glory, messiahship, and divine sonship), calling observers to faith.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A miraculous deed, wonder, or token performed by God or His authorized messengers that authenticates divine authority, reveals God's glory or presence, and is intended to produce faith or obedience

currentEntries.definition: The nations in turmoil — the raging sea, stilled at Christ's word, “Peace, be still”.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: divine judgment, and the trials of life which Christ has power to calm.
currentEntries.citations: (Ps 65:7; Isa 17:12-13; Mark 4:39; Luke 21:25) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Divine judgment or wrath arriving as overwhelming calamity. In prophetic and apocalyptic imagery, a storm or tempest commonly portrays God’s forceful visitation against sin, nations, or false security.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the storm or tempest most commonly symbolizes divine judgment and the wrath of God — an overwhelming manifestation of God's power breaking in upon human sin and rebellion. Closely bound to this is the theophanic sense: the storm as the vehicle or accompaniment of God's presence and speech. In devotional and homiletical use, the storm is also very widely applied to the trials, tribulations, and chaos of life that test faith, from which Christ delivers believers — an application anchored in the Gospel accounts of Jesus calming the storm.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: adversity, trials, tribulations, or times of distress that test faith

currentEntries.definition: God's law — the standard.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: Christ Himself, and God's word — the gospel that sets free.
currentEntries.citations: (Ps 119:142; 2 John 4) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: God’s revealed reality—supremely embodied in Jesus Christ and expressed in God’s word—standing in opposition to falsehood, deception, and sin.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'the truth' is understood primarily as God's self-revelation made known and embodied in Jesus Christ — not merely accurate information but the divine reality, faithfulness, and saving revelation of God, personified in Christ and communicated through his word and gospel. The most widely repeated formulation is that Jesus does not simply teach the truth but IS the truth, so that knowing the truth means knowing him and being rightly related to God, with liberating and sanctifying effect.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ as the personal embodiment and full revelation of divine truth

currentEntries.definition: The low and humbled — the opposite of the mountain-kingdom; “every valley shall be exalted”.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the low seasons of trial and death, set against the mountaintop.
currentEntries.citations: (Isa 40:4) · see Mountain, ch. 39 — derived in the digital edition’s symbol study at TimeTested.Bible

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: A low place of suffering, danger, grief, or spiritual trial through which God accompanies and sustains his people.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, the valley most commonly symbolizes a season of trial, suffering, darkness, or spiritual low point — the 'low place' of human experience (often contrasted with mountaintop experiences of blessing or divine encounter) through which God nevertheless accompanies and sustains the believer.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: A place or season of trial, affliction, spiritual darkness, or testing that the believer must pass through under God's care

currentEntries.definition: Covenant conduct — the walk.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: Jesus Himself as the one way to the Father; the narrow way against the broad.
currentEntries.citations: (Jer 6:16; Matt 7:14) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: The way of salvation and life with God, centered in Jesus Christ: Christ is the way to the Father, and following “the way” means trusting him and living as his disciple.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In Christian teaching, 'the Way' primarily symbolizes Jesus Christ himself as the exclusive path to God the Father and to salvation — access to God through the person, death, and resurrection of Christ. Closely bound to this, 'the Way' was the earliest self-designation of the Christian movement in Acts, so the term also stands for the whole Christian life of discipleship: following Jesus as both the road and the pattern of life that leads to God.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Jesus Christ as the exclusive path/means of access to God and salvation

currentEntries.definition: Deeds — not a synonym for obedience. A work becomes obedience when it executes a legitimate command; it becomes disobedience when the command or deed conflicts with God's command. Romans 4 uses the laborer's work offered for wages and debt; James 2 uses Abraham's work as faith made visible. Complete obedience still earns no wage: the servant has only done his duty.
currentEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: in Paul's salvation texts, “works” broadly includes human obedience and effort set against faith; good works then follow salvation as its fruit and evidence.
currentEntries.citations: (Ex 18:20; Ps 111:7; Mic 6:16; Luke 17:7-10; Rom 4:4-5; Jas 2:21-22) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6, for faith and works, and The End of the Law for Paul's works, wages, and duty vocabulary

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: “Works” most commonly means a person’s deeds or conduct as the outward expression and moral fruit of inward faith, character, and allegiance. Good works are acts of obedience, love, justice, and mercy; evil works are sinful acts that manifest unbelief or corrupt desire. They are frequently portrayed as evidence by which persons are known and judged, although Christian traditions differ over their precise relation to salvation.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, 'works' are understood as the outward deeds or actions of a person that express and evidence the inner spiritual condition — good works being the visible fruit of genuine faith, God's grace, and a regenerated heart, and evil works being the visible fruit of unbelief, the sinful nature ('the flesh'), or alignment with darkness. Works function as evidence or fruit rather than as the root: they reveal what a person truly is (a tree known by its fruit), and they will be the basis of divine assessment at judgment because they manifest the heart. In the dominant Protestant framing, good works are distinguished from saving faith — believers are saved by grace through faith, not by works, yet are saved 'unto' good works which necessarily follow true faith.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Human deeds/actions (good works as righteous fruit of genuine faith that evidence salvation and glorify God; evil works as sinful deeds of the flesh that reveal unbelief and bring judgment)

currentEntries.definition: Paul's phrase for deeds considered in relation to law. It is not a synonym for obedience and does not identify one unchanging class of deeds. The surrounding passage may identify God's law, a circumcision-party application, or leave the particular acts unnamed. What remains consistent is the rejected claim made for those deeds: they cannot purchase justification, produce the Spirit, establish covenant standing, or place God in debt. The context identifies the work; the phrase denies it as the purchase price.
currentEntries.citations: (Rom 3:20, 28; 9:32 KJV/TR; Gal 2:16; 3:2, 5, 10) · see The End of the Law

judges.label: GPT
judges.consensusMeaning: Deeds done in obedience to “the law,” ordinarily understood as the commandments of the Mosaic Torah, especially when relied upon as the basis or means of being justified before God. In much Christian teaching, the phrase consequently represents human law-keeping or religious achievement contrasted with justification by faith.

judges.label: Claude
judges.consensusMeaning: In mainstream Christian teaching, especially in the Reformation/Protestant tradition, 'works of the law' (Greek: erga nomou) refers to deeds performed in obedience to the Mosaic law—understood broadly as any human effort or moral/ritual performance undertaken to earn or establish righteousness before God. The phrase functions in Paul's letters as the negative pole in the faith-versus-works contrast: no one is justified by works of the law, but only through faith in Jesus Christ. Symbolically, the term stands for legalism, self-reliant human achievement, and works-righteousness as opposed to justification received by grace through faith.

judges.label: Grok
judges.consensusMeaning: Human efforts or deeds of obedience to the Mosaic Law (Torah) that cannot justify or make a person righteous before God, in contrast to justification by faith in Christ

glossaryEntries.definition: The watcher-tree and the priesthood's sign — first tree to wake, from shaqad, to watch: “I will watch over my word.” Aaron's dead rod budded, blossomed, and yielded almonds overnight — the house of Levi chosen by a resurrection sign — and the sanctuary lampstand is carved of almond cups: the watcher-tree bears the lamp.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Jer 1:11-12; Num 17:8; Ex 25:33-34) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

glossaryEntries.definition: To mark a person or thing as God's own and appoint it to a stated office or work. The oil may carry the visible mark; the Spirit may carry the power; the work declares what the appointment is for.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly used for the Holy Spirit's empowering presence, often without distinguishing appointment, sign, power, and office.

glossaryEntries.term: Assembly of the wicked / synagogue of Satan
glossaryEntries.definition: The counterfeit congregation — an edah (the covenant-assembly word) claiming covenant standing while gathered against the covenant's Lord: God names the rebel camp “this evil congregation… gathered together against me,” Korah's company declares all the congregation holy, and at the cross the assembly encloses the Messiah from inside the camp while the dogs compass from without — “the synagogue of Satan, which say they are Jews, and are not.”
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 22:16; Num 14:35; 16:3; Ps 1:5; 26:5; Acts 4:27; Rev 2:9; 3:9) · see What Is the Point?, ch. 25

glossaryEntries.definition: The self-made kingdom that builds a name against heaven — an empire raised over many kingdoms, the covenant counterfeit.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 11:4; Jer 51:7; Rev 17:18) · see The Bow, ch. 44, and The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

glossaryEntries.definition: The firstfruits — the first and humblest grain, reaped in spring; the sheaf waved before the LORD, which is Christ risen.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ex 9:31; Lev 23:10; Ruth 1:22; 2 Kgs 4:42; 1 Cor 15:20) · see Grass, ch. 42

glossaryEntries.definition: A nation or kingdom of the world — the wild, predatory figure of a people, as the tree is its rooted figure; different beasts are different kingdoms, and the unclean beasts are the Gentile nations God cleanses in Peter's vision.

Receiving God's testimony as governing truth in a response that submits to it. Bare assent can recognize a fact — demons believe and tremble — but saving belief obeys the word believed, and persistent refusal to obey exposes unbelief.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: personal trust in Christ, not mere assent — the instrument that receives salvation.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Mark 1:27; John 3:36; 12:42-43; Rom 10:16; Heb 3:18-19; Jas 2:19-22) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

glossaryEntries.definition: What a people is strung together by — a kingdom's covenant, and the might that is that covenant's outward face: one word (qesheth) carries weapon, might, and covenant-token, and to break the bow is to unstring the kingdom.
The curse-ground's crop — those consumed by “the care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches”: fruitless, choking the word, offering a false shadow, and ending in fire.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 3:18; Matt 13:22; Judg 9:15; 2 Sam 23:6-7; Heb 6:8) · see The Parables of the Kingdom, ch. 2

glossaryEntries.definition: The members of a nation — broken off, or grafted in, while the tree itself stands.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rom 11:17) · see Trees, ch. 41

glossaryEntries.definition: The word of God.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Deut 8:3; Matt 4:4) · see Orphans, Widows & the Fatherless, ch. 14

glossaryEntries.definition: The word churned solid — milk worked by labor into sound doctrine: the diet that teaches to “refuse the evil, and choose the good,” the remnant's food, the wash of the walking feet (“I washed my steps with butter”). Its counterfeit is speech “smoother than butter” with war beneath.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Prov 30:33; Isa 7:15, 22; Job 29:6; 2 Sam 17:29; Ps 55:21) · see Butter, ch. 47

glossaryEntries.term: Cast into the sea (a stone, mountain, or millstone sinking)
glossaryEntries.definition: The fall of Babylon — a ruling power irreversibly destroyed, sunk into the sea of peoples, never to rise. A phrase-symbol, not a single word.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Jer 51:63-64; Rev 18:21; Ex 15:4-5) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

glossaryEntries.definition: The towering tree — a power of great height and majesty, whoever bears it: Assyria was “a cedar in Lebanon”; the house of David the “high cedar” whose tender twig God replants to become “a goodly cedar”; the righteous “grow like a cedar.” The symbol is the stature, not the nation's identity.
The empty husk winnowed off the grain and driven away by the wind — what the wicked are likened to: weightless, rootless, blown off and burned. Not to be confused with the tares.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 1:4; Matt 3:12) · see Grass, ch. 42

glossaryEntries.definition: To cleanse is to remove the defilement that bars proper contact, approach, or use; clean describes what is free of that defilement and fit for its permitted place. Uncleanness may be physical, ceremonial, or moral and does not always mean guilt: childbirth, marital relations, and touching the dead all make unclean without being called sin. Cleansing removes what makes a vessel unfit; sanctification places the cleansed vessel under a holy claim and appointed use.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly treated either as hygiene and obsolete ritual regulation, or as a synonym for moral purity and holiness.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Lev 10:10; 12:2; 15:18; Num 19:11; Ps 51:2, 10; Eph 5:26; 1 John 1:7, 9) · see Uncommon Sanctification, Justification, and Cleanliness

glossaryEntries.definition: The vehicle of heaven — “who maketh the clouds his chariot” — and its cargo is the word: “my doctrine shall drop as the rain.” The pillar that led Israel, the cloud that received Him and brings Him back in like manner, the transport of the caught-up saints; risen from the sea of peoples, a multitude airborne — the cloud of witnesses. Its counterfeit is the cloud without water.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 104:3; Ex 13:21; Acts 1:9-11; Dan 7:13; 1 Thess 4:17; Heb 12:1) · see Clouds, ch. 37 | (Ps 104:3; Ex 13:21; Acts 1:9-11; Dan 7:13; 1 Thess 4:17; Heb 12:1) · see Clouds, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

glossaryEntries.definition: The stamped image — a person as the owner's minted image-bearer: dug from the field, refined in the fire, struck with the NAME; priced by the law, ransomed at a flat half-shekel when counted, lost and sought by lamplight. Man's mint valued the Shepherd at slave-damages; God's scales weigh the widow's whole living above all abundance.
Concealed disobedience — deeds hidden from the light.
glossaryEntries.citations: (John 3:19-20) · see Light and Darkness, ch. 21

glossaryEntries.definition: The time of light — exposure and accountability, when deeds are seen and tested; the season to walk, work, and watch. The children of light are the children of the day. In the prophets’ counts the day is a unit that scales: a day for a year in judgment, and one day with the Lord as a thousand years.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 1:5; John 9:4; 1 Thess 5:5; Num 14:34; Ezek 4:6; 2 Pet 3:8) · see Light and Darkness, ch. 21

glossaryEntries.definition: One in whom the law is sealed — “seal the law among my disciples” — proven by continuing in the word, love, and fruit; three times Jesus says cannot of those who will not leave their own, bear the cross, and forsake all. Baptized into the Name, the disciple is perfected “as his master” — the Head whose Name carries the Word, the covenant law, and the fruitful priesthood.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: a learner and follower of Jesus — any believer, entered by faith and baptism, growing lifelong in Christlikeness.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 8:16; Luke 6:40; Ex 23:21; Jer 31:33; John 8:31; Luke 14:26-33; Rev 14:1) · see The Disciple, ch. 9

glossaryEntries.definition: The covenant lawsuit executed — the wife sent out of the house: exile and scattering. Hated when it betrays the wife of the covenant; commanded when the union is itself fornication — a marriage God never joined. God gave Israel the bill, and answered His own no-return rule at the cross.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Jer 3:8; Isa 50:1; Deut 24:1-4; Ezra 10:3; Mal 2:11-16) · see Marriage and Divorce, ch. 12

glossaryEntries.definition: The Gentile power — an unclean beast outside the covenant table, fed on the crumbs that fall from it until brought in; at the cross it was the dogs that compassed and pierced, and at the end, without are dogs.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 15:26-27; Mark 7:28; Ps 22:16; Rev 22:15) · see Trees, ch. 41

glossaryEntries.definition: The destination of the way — the entrance to the house of God, marked on the posts.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ex 12:7; Deut 6:9; John 10:9) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

glossaryEntries.definition: A devouring kingdom.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: Satan himself, per Revelation 12:9.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Pharaoh, Ezek 29:3; Babylon, Jer 51:34) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4

glossaryEntries.definition: The front of the compass — Hebrew qedem, “east” and “ancient” in one word: Eden planted eastward, the glory returning “from the way of the east,” the lightning of the coming, the kings of the east crossing the dried river. Where beginnings and returns come from.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 2:8; Ezek 43:2; Matt 24:27; Rev 16:12; Ezek 46:1) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

glossaryEntries.definition: Spiritually, the whore of Babylon that rides the beast — the city that kills the prophets, “where also our Lord was crucified”: Jerusalem.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: bondage to sin, and the world-system out of which God redeems.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rev 11:8; 18:24; Matt 23:37; Gal 4:25; Isa 1:10) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

glossaryEntries.definition: Babel’s confederate — allied with Shinar in Scripture's first war, judged under Babylon's own sentence (“I will break the bow of Elam”), its oracle the prologue to Babylon's fall.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 14:1, 9; Jer 49:35; 51:56) · see The Bow, ch. 44

glossaryEntries.definition: The leaders of the assemblies, seated among the host of heaven — the court round about the throne, the named and brightest of the stars.
glossaryEntries.citations: (1 Kgs 22:19; Isa 24:23; Rev 4:4; Matt 19:28; Ps 89:5-7) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

glossaryEntries.definition: The scattered firstborn whose seed becomes the fulness of the nations.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 48:19) · see Jacob, Israel & Ephraim, ch. 45

glossaryEntries.definition: The lamp of the body — a burning light within a person, shining as the stars shine; the good eye gives its bread to the poor, the evil eye withholds; His eyes are flames of fire, running to and fro through all the earth.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 6:22-23; Prov 22:9; 23:6; Zech 4:10; Rev 1:14; 5:6) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

glossaryEntries.definition: Trusting faithfulness — reliance on God's unseen promise held steady through obedience. Works do not purchase the promise; they enact and bring faith to maturity, and faith without them is dead.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: confident trust in God and His promises — the sole instrument of justification.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Hab 2:4; Heb 11:1, 8; Jas 2:17, 22; Rom 4:4-5; Eph 2:8-10) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

glossaryEntries.definition: The Messiah — the one who bears the Father's light unchanged through the night; the moon is that name written in the sky, His throne established in the heavens.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 89:37; Rev 1:5; 3:14; Isa 55:4) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

glossaryEntries.definition: God's covenant people left without their Father — the remnant.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Lam 5:3) · see Orphans, Widows & the Fatherless, ch. 14

glossaryEntries.definition: Reverent awe expressed as keeping the commandments and departing from evil.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Eccl 12:13) · see The Fear of the Lord, ch. 23

glossaryEntries.definition: The walk — a man's conduct, his way; washed clean while the body stays bathed.
glossaryEntries.citations: (John 13:10) · see Garments & Armor, ch. 43

glossaryEntries.definition: The world — Jesus’ own decoding — sown with the seed of the word and reaped at the harvest; its unreaped edge is where the poor and stranger glean, and its hidden treasure is bought whole to be mined.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 13:38; Lev 19:9-10) · see Grass, ch. 42

glossaryEntries.definition: Self-made righteousness — a covering of one's own cut, all show and no substance; the cursed fig tree bore leaves but no fruit.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 3:7; Matt 21:19) · see Garments & Armor, ch. 43

glossaryEntries.definition: God's own consuming presence — “the LORD thy God is a consuming fire”: never a chamber, always the encounter. The same fire sustains the bush, refines the silver, walks the covered out of the furnace, and consumes the uncovered; the difference is never the fire but the covering.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Deut 4:24; Heb 12:29; Ex 3:2; Dan 3:25-27; Mal 3:3; 1 Cor 3:15) · see Heaven and Hell, ch. 16

glossaryEntries.definition: The divider God set between the two seas of people — the restless nations below and the gathered waters above, the heavenly assembly — and the place where the lights are hung.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 1:6-8, 14-17; Ps 148:4; Rev 17:15) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

glossaryEntries.definition: Men in the sea of nations — and the redeemed drawn out of it, the catch of the fishers of men gathered in the net.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Hab 1:14; Matt 4:19; 13:47-48) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

glossaryEntries.definition: A great ruler among the sea of peoples — the personal head who can stand for the kingdom, state, and administration acting through him. Pharaoh stands for Egypt, Nebuchadnezzar for Babylon, and Caesar for Rome: the ruler swallows through the body he heads, and is forced to give back what he swallowed.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: God's appointed rescue-instrument, a type of the three days in the tomb.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ezek 29:3; 32:2; Jer 51:34, 44; Dan 7:17, 23; John 19:15-16) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4

glossaryEntries.definition: An army in motion — a nation invading, or the Lord's own host sweeping the enemy away.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 8:7; Jer 47:2; Dan 9:26) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

glossaryEntries.definition: One who hears God's word and will not do it — the lawless, not the unintelligent.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 14:1; Matt 7:26) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20

glossaryEntries.definition: The blocking flesh — “the body of the sins of the flesh,” Scripture's own decode — covering a covenant member and stopping its work: the uncircumcised heart cannot be humbled or love, the uncircumcised ear “cannot hearken,” uncircumcised lips cannot be heard, and a young tree's fruit is “uncircumcised” until the covenant year. Cut it away, or be cut off.
Spiritual unfaithfulness — breaking covenant with God to go after other gods and kingdoms; not merely the physical sin. The out-of-covenant union is itself the whoredom.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ex 34:15-16; Hos 1:2; Jer 3:9; Rev 17:2) · see Marriage and Divorce, ch. 12

glossaryEntries.definition: The four spirits of heaven — God's executing agents, shown as the four horsemen.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Zech 6:5) · see The Four Winds, ch. 34

glossaryEntries.definition: A nation's works, by which it is judged — “every good tree bringeth forth good fruit”.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 7:17; 21:43) · see Trees, ch. 41

glossaryEntries.definition: A planted stand of trees — a grouping of nations.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: paradise and fellowship with God — Eden lost and restored.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ezek 31:9) · see Trees, ch. 41

glossaryEntries.definition: Righteousness — the righteous acts of the saints.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rev 19:8, ASV) · see Garments & Armor, ch. 43

glossaryEntries.definition: The judgment — the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem's wall, where the carcases of the transgressors burn: “their worm shall not die, neither shall their fire be quenched.” What destroys “both soul and body,” distinct from Sheol, the grave that holds all alike.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 10:28; Isa 66:24; Jer 7:32; Mark 9:43-48) · see Heaven and Hell, ch. 16

glossaryEntries.definition: The rage of the wicked at the righteous — what the excluded do at the sight of the kingdom they forfeited, sorrow and hatred in one face; then they melt away. Defined on the wicked against the just, staged at Stephen's trial, templated in the psalm: he shall see, be grieved, gnash, and perish.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the anguish of the damned under conscious, everlasting torment.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 112:10; Ps 37:12; Luke 13:28; Acts 7:54; Matt 8:12) · see The Weeping and the Gnashing | (Ps 112:10; Ps 37:12; Luke 13:28; Acts 7:54; Matt 8:12) · see The Weeping and the Gnashing, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

glossaryEntries.definition: The gospel of the kingdom — the renewed covenant, the law going forth from Zion.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the good news that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 52:7; 2:3; Jer 31:33; Heb 4:2) · see Gospel, ch. 5

glossaryEntries.definition: Favor that moves first — “while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” — and then goes to work: “teaching us that, denying ungodliness… we should live soberly, righteously, and godly.” Its counterfeit turns it into license (Jude 4).
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: unmerited favor — “getting what you don't deserve” — with no office afterward.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rom 5:8; Titus 2:11-12; Ex 34:6) · see Grace, Mercy & the Gift, ch. 24

glossaryEntries.definition: The wild branch — the stranger, the Gentile — received into the covenant tree.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rom 11:17) · see Trees, ch. 41

glossaryEntries.definition: A nation's works ripened into its people — persons as the vineyard's yield: God looked for grapes — judgment and righteousness — and found men: Israel “like grapes in the wilderness,” the good man the missing cluster, the remnant the blessing left in it. Pressed, the grape gives blood — the cup of the covenant, or the cup of wrath, as the vintage is grapes or wild grapes.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 5:2-7; Hos 9:10; Mic 7:1-2; Isa 65:8; Gen 49:11; Rev 14:18-20) · see The Parable of the Vineyard | (Isa 5:2-7; Hos 9:10; Mic 7:1-2; Isa 65:8; Gen 49:11; Rev 14:18-20) · see The Parable of the Vineyard, in the free digital edition at TimeTested.Bible

glossaryEntries.definition: The individual mortal — a man, flesh; and the field God farms unto harvest.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 40:6-8; Matt 13:38) · see Grass, ch. 42

glossaryEntries.definition: The covenant-breaker who wears the form of covenant without its substance — “that great city,” spiritually Sodom, Egypt, Babylon: Jerusalem unfaithful.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: spiritual adultery; in Revelation, an apostate religious world-system — Rome, not Jerusalem.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rev 17:18; 11:8; Ezek 23:19) · see The Fall of Babylon, ch. 35

glossaryEntries.definition: The end of the age, when the field of mankind is reaped — the wheat gathered, the chaff burned.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Joel 3:13; Matt 13:39) · see Grass, ch. 42

glossaryEntries.definition: To un-choose — the repudiation of a covenant partner or claim, never a mere feeling: the un-favored wife, the ground of divorce, the King refused. Scripture glosses it by its enactments — sent away, driven out of the house, “did not choose,” “I will love them no more” — and keeps the grudge in other words (satam, natar); Jesus' parallel saying translates the hard text: “hate not” father and mother is “he that loveth father or mother more than me.”
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: an emotion — hostility, bitterness — softened in the famous texts to “love less.”
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 29:30-31; Prov 1:29; Hos 9:15; Luke 14:26) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

glossaryEntries.definition: Jerusalem — the navel and heart of the land.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the grave or Hades, where Christ lay three days.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 12:40; Ezek 5:5; 38:12) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4, and The Ship

glossaryEntries.definition: The jurisdiction where God's will is already done — the visible sky and the seat of rule in one dual word (shamayim), over against the earth, the realm delegated to men where His will must yet be done. God's motion is downward — rain, fire, the Son, the city; the climb up is Babel's. The hope is heaven come down, not man gone up.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 115:16; Isa 66:1; Matt 6:10; John 3:13; Rev 21:2-3) · see Heaven and Hell, ch. 16

glossaryEntries.definition: One English word laid over two different things — Sheol/Hades, the grave that swallows righteous and wicked alike, and Gehenna, the judgment that destroys. The doctrine changes with the word beneath.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: the place of eternal conscious punishment and separation from God.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Ps 16:10 with Matt 10:28) · see Heaven and Hell, ch. 16

glossaryEntries.definition: The head covered with yeshuah — Yeshua: God's own war-dress, put on when there was no man, and lent to the soldier; David's form of it — “thou hast covered my head in the day of battle.” The head of every man is Christ, and the counterfeit is issued for the same forehead.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 59:16-17; Eph 6:11, 17; Ps 140:7; 1 Cor 11:3; 1 Thess 5:8; Rev 22:4) · see Garments & Armor, ch. 43

glossaryEntries.definition: The way of holiness — the prepared road home.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Isa 35:8) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

glossaryEntries.definition: The mount of an executing spirit; the conqueror who wins the nations by the bow.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rev 6:2) · see The Four Winds, ch. 34

glossaryEntries.term: Image of metals (gold, silver, brass, clay)
glossaryEntries.definition: The succession of gentile world-kingdoms, shattered by the stone-kingdom of God.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Dan 2:32-45) · see Mountain, ch. 39

glossaryEntries.definition: The discipline of the law, received and kept — what only fools despise.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Prov 1:7; 23:23) · see The Fool and the Wise, ch. 20

glossaryEntries.definition: The fourth kingdom — Rome: Daniel named Medo-Persia and Greece outright, and the iron that breaks in pieces all before it is the empire that held the world when He came.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Dan 2:40; 8:20-21) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4

glossaryEntries.definition: A set-apart, sanctified people — the covenant-rock risen out of the sea of nations (a mountain breaking the surface), waiting for the law that sanctifies it; “the island of the innocent,” delivered to safety while the kingdoms fall.
The new name of the one who prevails with God — covenant and character, not blood.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 32:28; Rom 9:6) · see Jacob, Israel & Ephraim, ch. 45

glossaryEntries.definition: The crooked, supplanting human heart that God transforms.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 27:36; Jer 17:9) · see Jacob, Israel & Ephraim, ch. 45

glossaryEntries.definition: In covenant contexts, one in the covenant — “he is a Jew, which is one inwardly,” while some “say they are Jews, and are not.” The name is Judah's, and Judah means praise — “Now will I praise the LORD” — so Paul's definition lands on the name itself: the Jew inwardly is he “whose praise is not of men, but of God.” The word also walks in plain dress, ethnic and religious; context decides which coat it wears.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Rom 2:28-29; Gen 29:35; Rev 3:9; Rom 9:6; Zech 8:23) · see Jacob, Israel & Ephraim, ch. 45

glossaryEntries.definition: The law's ruling and the ruler's office — what God declares due, kept like a commandment and owed first to the widow, the fatherless, the stranger, and the poor. To judge is to rule and deliver by the law (the judges were saviours; “a king to judge us… and fight our battles”), so the righteous pray for judgment and creation rejoices at its coming; condemnation is one verdict of the office, not the office.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Deut 10:18; Ps 119:160; Matt 23:23; 1 Sam 8:20; Isa 33:22; Dan 7:22) · see Justice and Judgment, ch. 18

glossaryEntries.definition: Righteousness under a second English name — one Hebrew word behind both renderings: the commandments done where a neighbor can be wronged or righted.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 18:19/Jer 22:3; Ps 89:14/97:2) · see Justice and Judgment, ch. 18

glossaryEntries.definition: To judge, declare, or demonstrate a person, word, deed, or cause right against a question or charge; the opposite is to condemn. God answers the charge against the sinner by grace through Christ, forgiving rather than renaming ungodliness righteousness. Deeds may vindicate a claimed faith, but they cannot purchase the Judge's mercy or place God in debt.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught in Protestant theology: God's once-for-all legal declaration that a believer is righteous through Christ's imputed righteousness, received by faith apart from works.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Deut 25:1; Prov 17:15; Matt 11:19; Luke 7:29; Rom 3:24-26; 4:4-8; 8:33; Jas 2:21-25) · see Uncommon Sanctification, Justification, and Cleanliness, and The End of the Law for Paul's law, works, wages, and debt vocabulary

glossaryEntries.definition: Covenant relationship proven by obedience — the intimate “knew” of marriage; a stranger is one not known.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 4:1; Hos 4:6; Matt 7:23; 1 John 2:3-4) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

glossaryEntries.definition: One of the flock — a covenant person, not by itself Christ: Nathan's ewe lamb is a poor man's beloved, Jeremiah is “like a lamb… brought to the slaughter,” the disciples are sent “as lambs among wolves.” The Lamb of God is Christ — the one lamb “without blemish,” taken “out from the sheep”: the perfect lamb of the flock.
glossaryEntries.citations: (2 Sam 12:3; Jer 11:19; Isa 53:6-7; Ex 12:5; Luke 10:3; John 1:29) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7 — derived in the digital edition’s symbol study at TimeTested.Bible

glossaryEntries.definition: The commandment.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Prov 6:23) · see Light and Darkness, ch. 21

glossaryEntries.definition: Bread soured — the word made impure, embittered, and puffed up; the hidden corruption that ferments through the whole lump, purged before Passover and forbidden on God's altar. The NT names it the corrupt doctrine of the Pharisees.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Lev 2:11; Matt 16:12; 1 Cor 5:7-8) · see Grass, ch. 42

glossaryEntries.definition: The King's jubilee release — out of the slaver's house (sin, Egypt, Babylon) and home to the household, inheritance, and service of God; a change of masters, never the absence of one. Its constitution is the perfect law of liberty; its counterfeit, liberty as license, is a return to bondage.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Lev 25:10; Isa 61:1; Jas 1:25; 2 Pet 2:19) · see Liberty, ch. 19

glossaryEntries.definition: Covenant existence — the life the law produces.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: Christ Himself, and the eternal life imparted to believers.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Deut 30:19-20; Lev 18:5; John 14:6; Matt 7:14) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7

glossaryEntries.definition: The law lived visibly — good works others can see.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Prov 6:23; Matt 5:16) · see Light and Darkness, ch. 21

glossaryEntries.definition: The devouring ruler or empire — the beast-kingdom at its most royal and most predatory: “as a roaring lion… so is a wicked ruler”; the princes are lions, and Assyria and Babylon “the lions” that scattered the sheep. The figure's rightful holder is the Lion of the tribe of Juda — and in His kingdom the lion is tamed.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Prov 28:15; Zeph 3:3; Jer 50:17; Ezek 19; Rev 5:5) · see The Way, the Truth & the Life, ch. 7 — derived in the digital edition’s symbol study at TimeTested.Bible

glossaryEntries.definition: A nation — as the beasts of Daniel's sea are kingdoms, the living creatures in Revelation's sea are peoples.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Dan 7:3, 17; Rev 8:9; 16:3) · see The Bow, ch. 44

glossaryEntries.definition: The Spirit and word of God going out to give life.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Jer 2:13; John 7:38) · see Sea & Waters, ch. 40

glossaryEntries.definition: The scattered house of Israel, sought and regathered.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Matt 15:24) · see Jacob, Israel & Ephraim, ch. 45

glossaryEntries.definition: Self-giving covenant allegiance embodied, for those under God's authority, in commandment-keeping. Obedience without love can be empty sacrifice, but claimed love that persistently refuses His commands is false — “this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments”.
glossaryEntries.commonView: Commonly taught: self-giving devotion or benevolence toward God and neighbor, with obedience as its necessary fruit and evidence rather than love's defining form.
glossaryEntries.citations: (John 14:15; 1 Cor 13:3; 1 John 4:8-10; 5:3; 2 John 4-6; Rom 13:10) · see Love, Knowing, Faith & Belief, ch. 6

glossaryEntries.definition: The covenant union of God and His people — the one-flesh bond God joins: the wife called by the Husband's name, brought under His wing.
glossaryEntries.citations: (Gen 2:24; Ezek 16:8; Eph 5:31-32; Rev 19:7) · see Marriage and Divorce, ch. 12
